chunks.content: Introduction ACJ dislocation is a common sports injury that occurs frequently, especially in young contact athletes [ ]. Studies have reported that up to 41% of college football players and 40% of NFL quarterbacks have experienced at least one ACJ dislocation during their careers. In addition, a significant number of ACJ injuries have been reported in non-contact sports such as cycling or triathlon [ , ]. The most common mechanism for ACJ dislocation is direct force on the shoulder during a fall in an arm-in-the-arm stance. The ACJ dislocations is a complex true synovial joint whose anatomy and function are critical to much of the motion of the arm and scapula. Despite the strength of its structure to withstand a large number of forces, the ACJ dislocations is susceptible to injury [ , ]. According to the Rockwood classification system, ACJ dislocations are categorized into six grades, of which types I and II are usually treated nonsurgically, while types IV through VI usually require surgical intervention. However, the optimal treatment of type III injuries is widely debated [ , ]. Imaging techniques play an important role in the diagnosis of ACJ dislocations, helping the surgeon to accurately assess the extent and type of injury so that an appropriate treatment plan can be developed [ ]. In recent years, advances in surgical techniques have led to more diverse approaches to the treatment of ACJ dislocations, but there are still differing views on the optimal timing and technique for different levels of injury. Rehabilitation is critical to recovery from ACJ dislocation, whether surgical or non-surgical treatments are used [ , ]. Rehabilitation programs include rest, pain management, and muscle strength and flexibility training aimed at restoring joint function and reducing recurrence. However, there is still a lack of adequate scientific validation of the effectiveness of different rehabilitation strategies and best practice guidelines [ ]. The aim of this review is to provide the latest perspectives and clinical guidelines for the treatment of ACJ dislocation by systematically reviewing the relevant literature and providing a comprehensive discussion and analysis of the background, epidemiology, anatomy, mechanism of injury, imaging, treatment and rehabilitation strategies (Fig. ). Anatomical basis and biomechanics of the ACJ Anatomical basics The acromioclavicular joint (ACJ) is stabilised chiefly by the acromioclavicular ligament, the two limbs of the coracoclavicular ligament (conoid and trapezoid), and the surrounding joint capsule [ ]. The ACJ, which connects the distal part of the clavicle to the acromioclavicular eminence of the scapula, is a complex, planar, synovial joint that permits a wide range of shoulder motions. The ACJ allows 5–8 mm translation and ~ 40° clavicular posterior rotation, movements essential for overhead function. Post-traumatic stability depends on three ligaments only: the AC-capsular, the conoid limb, and the trapezoid limb. AC-capsular ligament: primary restraint to anteroposterior shear; rupture produces horizontal instability requiring suture or figure-8 tape [ ]. Conoid limb: fails first in upward shear, and CC gap > 100%, needs vertical reconstruction [ , ]. Trapezoid limb: limits AP swing and axial rotation; intact limb allows conservative care in Rockwood II. Together with the dorsal capsule, they stabilise the joint and supply tissue for augmentation during surgery [ ]. The coracoacromial ligament, on the other hand, is divided into two parts: the conical ligament is located posteriorly and provides the main resistance to stress, and the trapezoidal ligament is located anteriorly and is more extensively involved in the vertical and horizontal stabilization of the joint. These ligaments, in combination with the joint capsule, provide the necessary stability to the ACJ and support the complex movements of the shoulder during high intensity activities [ , ]. Biomechanical basis Multiplanar coupling of slide and rotation optimises force transfer; over-constraining this (e.g., oversize hook plate) causes anterior-shoulder pain and loss of elevation [ ]. It allows the upper extremity to adapt to a variety of movements, thereby optimizing force transfer and movement efficiency. Dynamic stabilisers (trapezius, deltoid) provide > 50% of shear resistance between 0°–90° abduction. Deltoid weakness ≥ 20% doubles loss-of-reduction risk after single-button repair [ ]. The activity of these muscles helps to regulate and complement the stabilizing effect of the static ligaments, especially during exercise. Untreated vertical instability narrows the subacromial space by 2–4 mm and precipitates secondary impingement; early anatomical reduction restores ~ 80% of this clearance [ ]. For example, changes in the position of the clavicle can affect the subacromial space and may lead to conflict or other shoulder disorders. For example, changes in the position of the clavicle can affect the subacromial space and may lead to conflict or other shoulder disorders. Shoulder motion depends not only on static ligament support, but also on the coordinated work of dynamic muscle groups, such as the trapezius and deltoid, whose activity helps to regulate and supplement the stabilizing effects of the ligaments, especially when the shoulder is subjected to external forces or when it is engaged in a wide range of motion [ ]. The ACJ allows for subtle sliding and rotation of the clavicle over the acromion during complex movements such as throwing or elevating the arm, and this ability is key to maintaining the integrity of the upper extremity kinetic chain. When an ACJ injury such as dislocation occurs, this fine motor coordination is disrupted, which can lead to pain, limited motion, and long-term dysfunction [ , ]. Physical examination and imaging of ACJ Mechanism of ACJ dislocation ACJ dislocation is mainly caused by direct or indirect external forces. Direct external forces are usually due to an impact on the lateral aspect of the shoulder, such as a direct fall or impingement, which compresses the ACJ [ ]. Indirect external forces, on the other hand, are often due to a fall with the arm extended or elbow flexed, where the force is transmitted through the humeral head to the acromion, resulting in dislocation. In addition, the relative superficiality and lack of muscular protection of ACJ dislocations and the coracoclavicular ligament (CCL) make these structures susceptible to damage on impact [ ]. Physical examination Visual observation: Examine the shoulder for swelling, deformity, or skin lesions and assess the position of the acromion relative to the clavicle [ , ]. Palpation: Palpate along the acromioclavicular joint and surrounding structures, searching for pressure points, abnormal protrusions or displacement of the clavicle. Specific diagnostic tests: Transverse Arm Adduction Test: This test looks for specific ACJ pathology by asking the patient to bend the elbow, elevate the arm at 90 degrees and then retract it across the chest [ ]. O’Brien’s Test: The patient elevates the arm at 90 degrees, straightens the elbow and retracts it at 15 degrees, with the thumb downward, applying downward pressure [ , ]. The patient then externally rotates the arm and repeats the pressure test to compare changes in pain to diagnose ACJ injury. Paxinos sign: considered positive when pain is elicited by the examiner placing the thumb on the posterior-lateral aspect of the acromion and the fingers of the other hand pressed against the supraclavicular region, applying a squeezing pressure [ ]. ACJ classification Rockwood Classification: Type I injury: only the acromioclavicular ligament is injured and the ACJ remains stable. Type II injury: the acromioclavicular ligament is ruptured, the CC ligament remains intact, and the acromioclavicular space may be slightly widened. Type III injury: both the acromioclavicular and the CC ligaments are ruptured, and there is a complete subluxation of the clavicle in relation to the acromion, but there is no more than 100% widening of the CC space. Type IV injury: Posterior displacement of the distal clavicle, possibly into or through the trapezius fascia. Type V injury: significant acromioclavicular subluxation with a 100–300% increase in the CC gap. Type VI injury: inferior displacement of the distal clavicle to a subacromial or subrostrual position [ , ]. Here, we plot an example of ACJ Classification. Type V (severe superior displacement; CC distance increased 100–300% compared with contralateral side, often with deltotrapezial fascia disruption): rupture of the AC and CC ligaments, supination of the clavicle > 100%, with avulsion of the deltoid and trapezius origins. Clinical example: strong external forces in a car accident, doubling of the CC spacing on X-ray, intraoperative reconstruction with tendon grafts. Clinical example: Rare pattern of impingement with subclavian impingement below the coracoid process on CT. Imaging evaluation: defining injury patterns and guiding management The primary objectives of imaging in acromioclavicular joint (ACJ) dislocation are to (i) establish injury severity (Rockwood classification), (ii) quantify both vertical and—critically—horizontal instability, and (iii) translate measurable imaging findings into actionable treatment decisions, particularly for distinguishing Rockwood type III subtypes (IIIA vs. IIIB) [ ]. First-line imaging: standardized radiographic protocol Plain radiographs remain the cornerstone of initial assessment. A standardized, bilateral protocol is recommended: [ ]. Bilateral Upright Zanca View (AP, 10–15° cephalic tilt): This view optimizes visualization of the acromioclavicular joint (ACJ) itself. When performed as a bilateral stress view with standardized loading (e.g., 10 kg), it allows for quantification of the coracoclavicular (CC) distance. The CC distance on the injured side is compared to that on the contralateral, uninjured side, and the Rockwood classification is applied based on the calculated percentage of side-to-side widening. The established thresholds are: Type I (minimal or no widening, < 10%), Type II (partial disruption, 10% to ≤ 25% widening), Type III (complete disruption, > 25% to ≤ 100% widening), and Type V (severe displacement, > 100% widening) [ ]. True Axillary View: Essential for assessing static posterior displacement of the distal clavicle, which is consistent with the Rockwood type IV injury pattern. As interpretation is sensitive to projection and positioning, findings should be supported by strict technique and, when uncertain, corroborated with dynamic views [ , , ]. Stress Views (Selective Use): When vertical instability is equivocal on standard views, bilateral stress radiographs with standardized loading (e.g., 10 kg) can improve side-to-side comparability. Their routine use is debated, and they are best employed as a targeted adjunct within a diagnostic protocol rather than a universal screening tool. Quantifying horizontal instability: dynamic/functional radiography Since horizontal instability is frequently dynamic and under-recognized on static images, targeted functional radiography is central to accurate diagnosis and subtyping, particularly for type III injuries. Alexander (Lateral Stress) View: A stress radiographic view designed to assess for dynamic posterior translation (DPT), a key component of horizontal instability of the distal clavicle [ ]. Functional Axillary Series & GACA Quantification: A more quantitative approach involves obtaining dynamic axillary views in two positions: one with the arm in 90° of abduction and another with the arm in 90° of abduction plus approximately 60° of flexion or extension. The difference in the gleno-acromio-clavicular angle (GACA) between these two views is used to quantify horizontal (anteroposterior) translation of the clavicle, thereby assisting in the diagnosis of horizontal instability in acute AC joint injuries [ ]. Advanced imaging: when and why it changes management Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI): Best reserved for (i) evaluating suspected concomitant soft-tissue or intra-articular pathology (e.g., labral, rotator cuff injury), (ii) cases where precise appraisal of AC/CC ligament integrity could alter management counseling, or (iii) patients with persistent symptoms and discordant clinical-radiographic findings. MRI may provide additional information on injury severity compared with radiography alone and may influence treatment decision-making in selected cases. Computed Tomography (CT): Not indicated for routine grading of isolated ligamentous injury. Its value lies in clarifying complex osseous anatomy or horizontal malalignment when radiographic views are suboptimal, particularly for preoperative planning. Imaging-to-treatment translation: the practical value of quantification The ultimate utility of imaging lies in converting measurements into clear management pathways. Rockwood Typing with Measurable Parameters: Vertical severity is quantified by CC distance widening, while horizontal severity is assessed via static axillary and dynamic functional views. Differentiating Type IIIA vs. IIIB (The Critical Subdivision): Guided by ISAKOS consensus, type III injuries are stratified into a horizontally stable (IIIA) phenotype and a functionally unstable (IIIB) phenotype. Rockwood Typing with Measurable Parameters: Vertical severity is quantified by CC distance widening, while horizontal severity is assessed via static axillary and dynamic functional views. Differentiating Type IIIA vs. IIIB (The Critical Subdivision): Guided by ISAKOS consensus, type III injuries are stratified into a horizontally stable (IIIA) phenotype and a functionally unstable (IIIB) phenotype. The IIIA phenotype is characterized by the absence of clavicular overriding on dynamic stress views and no clinically relevant scapular dyskinesis, supporting a trial of non-operative care. Conversely, the IIIB phenotype is defined by radiographic evidence of clavicular overriding combined with clinical scapular dyskinesis—a pattern where surgical stabilization should be strongly considered in symptomatic patients [ , ]. Prognostic Relevance of Quantitative Instability: Measurable instability correlates with clinical outcomes; for example, higher vertical displacement (CCD) and more pronounced horizontal translation on Alexander views have been associated with inferior ACJ-specific scores in clinical cohorts. Assessment of Types IV-VI: While radiographs can demonstrate posterior displacement patterns and more severe injury types, accurate assessment of type IV remains challenging and depends on high-quality imaging to avoid projection artifact and misclassification. Treatment of ACJ dislocation The choice of treatment strategy for acromioclavicular joint (ACJ) dislocation has long been controversial. The core debates primarily focus on defining the indications for conservative versus surgical management, as well as the ongoing optimization of surgical techniques. Based on current evidence-based medicine, there is a general consensus that conservative treatment should be the first choice for stable Rockwood Types I, II, and IIIa injuries, whereas active surgical intervention is recommended for unstable Rockwood Types IIIb, IV, and V injuries. Low-grade injuries: Type I and Type II injuries: For both type I and type II ACJ dislocations, the common treatment is conservative, including the use of a sling to relieve pain and support the shoulder [ ]. According to a retrospective study by Park et al., patients with type I injuries require immobilization for an average of 19.5 days, with some patients reporting persistent symptoms at 6 weeks post-injury, while patients with type II injuries typically require longer immobilization, averaging 27 days [ , ]. Further retrospective data showed that while most patients responded well to nonsurgical treatment, 52% of patients with type I and type II injuries experienced at least occasional symptoms during follow-up, and one study with long-term follow-up (average 6.2 years) found that symptoms persisted in 48% of patients with type II injuries, and 27% ultimately opted for surgical treatment [ , ]. Type III injuries: non-surgical treatment༚The treatment of type III injuries is more controversial in the medical community. This injury involves rupture of the acromioclavicular and CC ligament with upward displacement of up to 100% of the width of the clavicle [ , ]. Although an initial attempt at non-surgical treatment, including immobilization in a sling for 4–5 weeks, is recommended in most cases for Type IIIa injuries, several randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses have found that the difference in clinical outcomes between surgical and non-surgical treatments, both in the short term and up to 20 years of follow-up, is not significant [ ]. Additionally, for high-function demand populations (e.g., young competitive athletes, military personnel), even Type IIIa injuries may require surgical consideration if conservative treatment fails to restore the required shoulder strength or stability. However, non-surgical treatments typically result in a faster and less costly return to work and daily activities. Nonetheless, some studies suggest that surgery may provide more stable anatomic reconstruction and reduce long-term pathologic changes, especially in athletes or in populations with high functional demands on the shoulder [ ]. For type III injuries, the consensus on the efficacy of nonsurgical treatment is unclear, although initially it was mostly recommended [ ]. Data from randomized controlled trials suggest that there is no significant difference in clinical outcomes between surgical and nonsurgical treatment of type III and type V injuries, either in the short term or at up to 18–20 years of follow-up [ ]. This finding is supported by another randomized controlled trial showing no difference in clinical outcomes at 24 months between surgical and non-surgical treatments for type III and type V injuries [ , ]. Meta-analysis further supports this, noting that while the surgical group may be better aesthetically, they have a longer time to disease progression. Surgical treatment: high-grade injuries (types IV, V, and VI)༚For more severe Type IV, V, and VI injuries, surgical treatment is often considered necessary to restore the anatomic position and function of the joint [ ]. Meta-analysis further supports this, noting that while the surgical group may be better aesthetically, they have a longer time to disease progression. Surgical treatment: high-grade injuries (types IV, V, and VI)༚For more severe Type IV, V, and VI injuries, surgical treatment is often considered necessary to restore the anatomic position and function of the joint [ ]. Relevant retrospective studies have shown that surgical treatment can lead to better clinical outcomes. For example, in one study, patients with type III injuries who underwent hook-and-plate surgical treatment had superior recovery outcomes in the surgical group compared to the nonsurgical treatment group [ ]. In addition, 92% of 46 patients with type III injuries who underwent surgical treatment in a long-term follow-up (21 years) study were satisfied with the outcome, suggesting that surgical treatment may provide a more stable recovery in some cases [ , ]. Analysis of the data on conservative and surgical treatments shows that the treatment strategy for ACJ dislocations should be based on the type of injury, the persistence of the patient’s symptoms, and his or her quality-of-life needs. Conservative treatment is recommended initially for type I and II injuries, with observation of symptomatic improvement [ ]. The treatment of type III injuries needs to be customized to the patient’s symptomatology and functional requirements, whereas, for severe injuries from type IV to VI, surgical treatment is often the preferred option to provide long-term stabilization and functional recovery [ ]. Surgical treatment options and approaches for ACJ dislocation Contemporary understanding of AC joint instability emphasizes that classification should inform treatment selection and outcome interpretation. Although the Rockwood system remains the most commonly used classification, an explicit treatment algorithm—particularly for Grade III—remains debated, and decision-making often incorporates patient-specific demands and the acute versus chronic setting. In chronic high-grade dislocations (> 3 weeks), surgical treatment is generally required to restore stability. Current surgical options can be conceptually grouped into (a) nonbiological coracoclavicular fixation (e.g., suture loops/synthetic constructs), (b) biological CC reconstruction (autograft/allograft), (c) tendon/ligament transfer, and (d) hardware-augmented reconstruction (e.g., hook plate or Bosworth screw) [ ]. This framework helps link classification with procedure selection and highlights trade-offs in outcomes and complications. In acute settings, fixation constructs are typically used to maintain reduction and facilitate native ligament healing, whereas chronic high-grade instability more often requires biological reconstruction. In addition, procedures differ in the primary instability plane addressed: coracoclavicular-based constructs primarily control vertical displacement, while persistent symptoms may reflect horizontal/rotational instability related to AC capsuloligamentous and deltotrapezial disruption, prompting consideration of concomitant AC/capsular management. Hook plate fixation and Bosworth screw fixation Hook plate fixation is a method commonly used to treat ACJ dislocations. The joint is kept in place by placing a fixation plate over the clavicle, with the hooked portion of the plate located below the acromion, and screws hold the plate in place over the clavicle [ ]. This technique is indicated for the treatment of acute ACJ dislocations with the goal of allowing the AC and CC ligaments to heal in a repositioned state. Studies have shown that hook plate fixation has better short-term results in Rockwood type III-V injuries, with a study by Kienast et al. showing good or excellent results in 89% of patients after hook plate fixation [ ]. However, hook plate fixation can lead to a number of serious complications, including subacromial osteolysis, upward cutting of the hook into the acromion, fractures, osteoarthritis of the ACJ, subacromial impingement, and rotator cuff tears [ ]. In addition, the biomechanics of the ACJ may change significantly after hook plate fixation, often requiring a second surgery to remove the fixation hardware [ ]. Bosworth screw fixation is another approach that maintains the joint in place by placing a screw between the clavicle and the coracoid process. This technique typically utilizes a 6.5 mm partially threaded cancellous screw that is inserted between the clavicle and the coracoid process to immobilize the joint [ , ]. Although Bosworth screw fixation showed good long-term results in initial reports, follow-up studies have noted that the high rate of fatigue and risk of fracture of the screws leads to technical failure, requiring a secondary procedure within 8–12 weeks of the initial surgery [ , ]. Anatomical and biological reconstruction The core objective of anatomical reconstruction is to precisely restore the natural attachment points and spatial orientation of the coracoclavicular (CC) ligaments, thereby reestablishing the physiological vertical and horizontal stability of the joint. The focus of its technical evolution lies in the progression from single-bundle to double-bundle reconstruction. This choice is not based on a single criterion but should be grounded in a comprehensive assessment of the patient’s individual circumstances and the injury mechanism. Considerations Based on Patient and Injury Factors: Patient Activity Demands and Occupational Requirements: For patients with high activity demands (e.g., athletes, manual laborers), double-bundle reconstruction demonstrates superior biomechanical stability, particularly in controlling anteroposterior translation, which is crucial for overhead activities. Body Mass Index (BMI) and Bone Quality: For patients with a BMI > 25 or poor bone quality, double-bundle reconstruction is recommended to distribute stress and reduce the risk of bone tunnel widening or fixation failure. If a single-bundle technique is used, augmentation with acromioclavicular ligament repair is advised to enhance stability. Dislocation Type and Injury Mechanism: For Rockwood type IV, V, or injuries with significant horizontal instability, double-bundle reconstruction—which effectively controls anterior-posterior translation—should be prioritized. Technical Rationale of Single-Bundle vs. Double-Bundle Reconstruction: Single-Bundle Reconstruction: Primarily simulates and restores the function of the original CC ligament (especially the conoid ligament), providing fundamental vertical stability. It is indicated for injuries with moderate instability [ ]. Double-Bundle Reconstruction: By separately reconstructing the two main bundles—the conoid and trapezoid ligaments—it provides more comprehensive anteroposterior and superior-inferior stability, making it suitable for highly unstable or severe ACJ injuries. Studies have shown that double-bundle fixation provides better vertical stability than single-bundle fixation. While American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) scores may be similar, double-bundle reconstruction performs better in maintaining the CC distance (CCIR score: 160.5% vs. 125.4%) [ ]. Biomechanical Advantages of the Double Cortical Button Anatomic (DCTa) Technique: Among double-bundle techniques, the Double Cortical Button Anatomic (DCTa) technique is favored for its ability to precisely replicate the native ligament attachment points and spatial orientation, thereby restoring physiological, multi-dimensional stability. Precise Control of Horizontal Instability: Biomechanical studies comparing anatomic (DCTa) versus non-anatomic double-tunnel configurations have demonstrated that the anatomic configuration results in significantly less total horizontal displacement under cyclic loading, highlighting that precise tunnel placement is key to restoring horizontal stability [ ]. Restoration of Physiological Constraints: The DCTa technique allows the conoid and trapezoid ligament bundles to function independently, with one primarily resisting posterior displacement and rotation, and the other synergistically controlling anterior displacement and providing vertical stability. This separate-bundle reconstruction more closely approximates the physiological state compared to single-bundle or conjoined techniques. In summary, the selection of anatomical reconstruction technique is an evidence-based decision process ranging from single-bundle to double-bundle. Double-bundle reconstruction, particularly the anatomically precise DCTa technique, offers a more reliable stability solution for high-demand patients and complex instability patterns through its biomechanical design that more closely approximates the physiological state. In chronic high-grade dislocations, whether reconstruction alone is sufficient or whether hardware augmentation improves stability and revision risk remains debated; a recent systematic review comparing these strategies may inform shared decision-making [ ]. Nonbiological coracoclavicular fixation Nonbiological coracoclavicular (CC) fixation refers to implant-based constructs designed to restore and maintain CC reduction without the use of tendon grafts. Suspension devices such as the TightRope, EndoButton, Dog Bone, and related systems are commonly used to shorten the CC distance and stabilize the ACJ, thereby facilitating healing of the injured AC and CC ligaments [ ]. These constructs are typically deployed with minimally invasive or arthroscopically assisted techniques, offering potential advantages such as reduced soft-tissue disruption, faster recovery, and improved cosmetic outcomes. However, implant-related complications remain a concern, including hardware migration or cut-through (with devices potentially breaching the clavicle or coracoid process), which may cause irritation and pain in the supraclavicular or coracoid region [ ]. Moreover, vertical placement of a single suspension device may not replicate the native CC ligament orientation and can be associated with persistent horizontal instability, as reported by Scheibel et al. In response, the use of two or more suspension devices has been advocated to better restore combined vertical and horizontal stability [ ]. Tunnel-related complications (including tunnel widening and coracoid/clavicle fracture) and loss of reduction remain important failure modes, particularly in bone-tunnel–based constructs. Ligament and/or tendon transfer procedures (Weaver–Dunn and Dewar) Ligament and/or tendon transfer procedures represent a historic but still clinically relevant category for the treatment of AC joint dislocation, particularly in chronic settings. The original Weaver–Dunn procedure (1972) involves distal clavicle resection and transfer of the coracoacromial ligament to the distal clavicle to reconstruct coracoclavicular restraint [ ]. Variations and “modified Weaver–Dunn” techniques typically aim to improve initial stability by adding supplemental fixation or reconstruction elements. However, when interpreted under current concepts of AC instability, tendon transfer procedures are generally considered non-anatomic and may be less reliable in restoring multidirectional stability compared with anatomic tendon-graft reconstruction. In a prospective comparative study in chronic cases, semitendinosus tendon graft CC reconstruction achieved significantly superior clinical and radiologic outcomes compared with a modified Weaver–Dunn procedure [ ]. The Dewar–Barrington procedure (1965) is another transfer-based strategy historically described for chronic AC dislocation, classically involving transfer of coracoid-based tissues to the clavicle to restore stability when other approaches fail [ ]. Although tendon transfer remains an option in selected circumstances (e.g., revision settings or when graft-based anatomic reconstruction is not feasible), comparative evidence in chronic high-grade instability suggests that tendon-graft reconstruction tends to yield better functional outcomes in higher-level studies. For example, a systematic review of chronic high-grade ACJ instability reported that, among level II studies, tendon graft reconstruction demonstrated superior results versus other categories (including tendon transfer), while overall complication rates were broadly comparable across groups [ ]. Open versus arthroscopic dissection techniques Open anatomical techniques focus on restoring biomechanical stability to the ACJ and usually involve reconstruction of the CC ligament and the AC ligament. The use of autologous or allogeneic grafts fixed through a tunnel between the clavicle and the coracoid process is aimed at restoring the anatomic and biomechanical function of the joint [ ]. Although the open dissection technique allows direct visualization of the joint and confirmation of horizontal stability, there are some risks such as graft rupture, rostral or clavicular fracture, and adhesive capsulitis [ ]. The arthroscopic dissection technique is a minimally invasive approach that focuses on surgical maneuvers through smaller incisions and arthroscopic equipment. Arthroscopic techniques typically offer the advantages of less soft tissue damage, less pain, shorter recovery time, and relatively lower complication rates than open techniques [ ]. Arthroscopically-assisted anatomic techniques are commonly used in the treatment of acute and chronic ACJ dislocations by means of a bicortical button technique in which the fixation device is passed through the clavicle and the coracoid process to keep the joint in place. The aim of this technique is to bring the joint into proximity at an early stage and to promote healing of the AC and CC ligaments.Accordingly, device-specific constructs and their complication patterns (including tunnel-related issues) are discussed in Sect. . The surgical treatment of ACJ dislocation is diverse and includes hook and plate fixation, Bosworth screw fixation, arthroscopically assisted CC fixation, open dissection techniques, and arthroscopic dissection techniques. Here, we summarize in detail the current mainstream surgical procedures for ACJ reconstruction. (Figures , , and ) Each surgical option has its advantages and risks, and the selection of an appropriate treatment option should be based on the severity of the injury, the patient’s needs, and the surgeon’s experience. Hook-and-plate fixation and Bosworth screw fixation are the traditional surgical approaches, but may require a secondary procedure to remove the hardware [ ]. Arthroscopic-assisted CC fixation techniques are popular because of their minimally invasive features, but the risk of hardware migration and vertical instability needs to be noted. Open anatomic and arthroscopic anatomic techniques focus on restoring anatomic stability to the joint, especially in more complex dislocation cases [ ]. Overall, treatment strategies should take into account the patient’s functional needs, surgical risks, and complication rates to achieve optimal clinical outcomes and patient satisfaction. (Table ) Common complications after ACJ dislocation treatment The risk of complications following ACJ dislocation treatment is closely related to the initial injury severity and the treatment modality selected. A comprehensive understanding of these risks is essential for shared decision-making with patients and for guiding the selection of surgical techniques aimed at minimizing specific complications. Complications of non-surgical treatment Non-surgical treatment for low-grade ACJ injuries shows a low complication rate, but the cosmetic results are usually poor. Some patients may experience shoulder pain and joint instability, but the overall complication rate is low. However, despite the low complication rate, attention needs to be paid to the impact on the patient’s appearance and potential long-term problems. Complications of surgical treatment A range of complications can occur when surgically treating ACJ instability, with reported rates ranging from 5% to 88.9% [ ]. A systematic evaluation by Woodmass et al. described the five most common complications following arthroscopic fixation of acromioclavicular separation as - Superficial infection: incidence of approximately 3.8% [ , ]. Shoulder pain: incidence of approximately 26.7%. Calcification of the rostral lock: incidence is about 31.6%. Fractures: incidence of approximately 5.3%. Loss of reduction: incidence of approximately 26.8%. Loss of repositioning after surgery is one of the most common complications, with an incidence ranging from 15% to 80% [ , ]. Loss of reduction is usually asymptomatic and does not interfere with return to pre-injury activity levels; therefore, the decision for revision surgery should be based on the patient’s clinical presentation rather than on imaging evidence alone. Postoperative Fractures and Hardware Displacement: rostral fractures may be caused by techniques that involve drilling tunnels into the coracoid process to place and immobilize grafts, with an incidence of up to 20% [ , ]. To minimize the risk of rostral fracture, it is recommended to use a small-diameter tunnel layout and avoid excessive drilling. Hardware displacement is relatively common and can lead to serious complications, such as hardware entering the pleural cavity, spinal canal, or carotid artery. The incidence of clavicle fractures varies, usually ranging from 4% to 43%. Tunneling into the clavicle to secure the graft increases the likelihood of fracture. To reduce the risk of clavicle fracture, the technique should minimize the diameter of the tunnel and rationalize the layout of the fixation points to reduce the risk of bone loss and fracture [ ]. Postoperative Infection and Calcification: The incidence of postoperative infection is low, usually in the superficial soft tissue range, and is more easily treated with medication. However, deeper infections involving the fixation device may be more serious and require more complex treatment regimens. Calcification of the rostral lock is another common complication, occurring in 50% to 80% of cases, with a variety of clinical presentations, but usually without affecting function or clinical outcome [ ]. Other Postoperative Complications: Osteoarthritis: Osteoarthritis may be part of the postoperative complications, especially if the procedure involves hardware fixation or resection of the distal clavicle. Osteoarthritis is not directly associated with unfavorable patient outcomes, but may trigger pain in some patients. Clavicle lysis: this is another relatively rare complication that may be related to hardware use or surgical technique. One possible cause is interruption of the blood supply to the clavicle periosteum, leading to distal bone loss [ ]. Surgical treatment of ACJ dislocations can have a variety of complications, and patients should be fully aware of these risks prior to treatment. Nonoperative treatment has a lower complication rate but may have a poorer cosmetic outcome; complications of surgical treatment may include loss of reset, rostral fracture, hardware displacement, infection, calcification, osteoarthritis, and clavicle lysis. The healthcare team should select the best treatment plan based on the patient’s clinical symptoms and individual circumstances, and should closely monitor postoperative complications for prompt intervention and treatment. (Table ) ACJ dislocation rehabilitation methods and programs Current rehabilitation protocols for ACJ dislocation are largely based on expert consensus, established clinical practice, and biomechanical principles, as high-level comparative evidence (e.g., randomized controlled trials) defining optimal timing and strategies remains limited. Therefore, the following phased framework should be considered a pragmatic, clinically oriented approach and individualized according to patient symptoms, stability (including suspected horizontal/rotational instability), functional goals, and response to therapy [ , ]. Core principles Successful rehabilitation emphasizes restoration of periscapular neuromuscular control and dynamic shoulder stability. Progression should be gradual and symptom-guided, with attention to scapular mechanics and kinetic-chain integration. Early phases should minimize maneuvers that generate horizontal shear across the AC joint—particularly cross-body adduction and resisted pushing/pulling—especially when horizontal instability is suspected. Core principles Successful rehabilitation emphasizes restoration of periscapular neuromuscular control and dynamic shoulder stability. Progression should be gradual and symptom-guided, with attention to scapular mechanics and kinetic-chain integration. Early phases should minimize maneuvers that generate horizontal shear across the AC joint—particularly cross-body adduction and resisted pushing/pulling—especially when horizontal instability is suspected. Close collaboration between the treating clinician and therapist is essential to align precautions with injury pattern and, when applicable, procedure-specific restrictions. Phase 1: immobilization & pain control (Approx. days 0–7 post-injury/non-op; days 0–10 post-op) Clinical Goals: Reduce pain and inflammation; protect healing tissues [ ]. Core Interventions: Sling for comfort and support; cryotherapy; active range of motion (AROM) for hand, wrist, and elbow; scapular setting as tolerated. Avoid early cross-body adduction, heavy lifting, and forceful pushing/pulling that may increase AC shear. Progression Criteria: Tolerates intermittent sling removal for hygiene and gentle pendulum exercises without significant pain [ ] (e.g., VAS ≤ 3 as a commonly used clinical threshold). Phase 2: early motion & scapular control (Approx. weeks 1–3 non-op; weeks 2–4 post-op) Clinical Goals: Restore comfortable ROM while maintaining stability; activate periscapular musculature. Core Interventions: Passive and active-assisted forward flexion and external rotation (typically progressed first in the scapular plane); closed-chain scapular stabilization exercises (e.g., scapular clocks). Cross-body adduction and other high-shear maneuvers should be avoided or introduced cautiously, particularly in patients with signs of horizontal instability or those undergoing combined vertical–horizontal stabilization [ ]. Progression Criteria: Achieves targeted ROM goals pain-free (e.g., flexion ~ 90° and ER ~ 30° as commonly used early targets), with no night pain and improving scapular control. Phase 3: strengthening—scapular & rotator cuff (Approx. weeks 3–6 non-op; weeks 4–8 post-op) Clinical Goals: Restore dynamic ACJ stability; normalize scapular kinematics; improve rotator cuff endurance and control. Core Interventions: Tubing rows; isometric to light isotonic rotator cuff strengthening; closed-chain serratus anterior drills (e.g., wall slides). Prone “T” and “Y” exercises may be introduced cautiously later in this phase if tolerated and scapular mechanics are controlled. Progression Criteria: Demonstrates symmetric scapular posture and control; achieves at least grade 4/5 manual muscle test strength in external rotation and scapular retraction (where MMT is used), without instability symptoms during functional tasks. Phase 4: functional & Sport-Specific training (Approx. weeks 6 + non-op; weeks 8 + post-op) Clinical Goals: Integrate the upper extremity kinetic chain; restore power and proprioception; prepare for return to full activity. Core Interventions: General: Progress to controlled push-ups and pressing patterns; if bench press is introduced, consider limiting provocative end-range lockout early; gradually reintroduce overhead pressing based on symptoms and stability. Throwing Athletes: Begin a structured interval throwing program (short distance/low intensity progressing stepwise) [ ]. Other Sports: Initiate sport-specific drills (e.g., groundstrokes, controlled serving) tailored to tolerance and mechanics. Progression Criteria: Full, pain-free ROM; successful completion of sport/work-specific functional tests; and strength/endurance and stability measures approaching the contralateral side (e.g., ~ 85–90% where objective testing is available). Progression through these phases should remain criteria-based rather than rigidly time-based and continuously adapted to the individual’s clinical presentation, stability profile, and functional milestones. The overarching aim is a safe and timely return to pre-injury activities while minimizing the risk of recurrent symptoms, re-injury, or chronic dysfunction.Here, we summarize recovery times and options for surgical and non-surgical treatments. (Table ) Discussion and conclusion Almost all of the relevant studies on ACJ injury currently have some limitations, and analyzing these issues can provide key ideas for future diagnosis and treatment. First, in the Anatomy and Biomechanics section, we point out that most of the studies relied on cadaveric specimens or in vitro models and lacked in vivo dynamic functional imaging and kinematic data for accurate and direct use in clinical analysis. Second, in the imaging evaluation, there is a high degree of heterogeneity among studies in terms of X-ray position, stress Zanca, CT/MRI parameters, and staging criteria, and the lack of uniform quantitative indexes is a key challenge that exists. In the future, uniform quantitative criteria are developed to improve the consistency of staging and diagnostic decisions. Again, among the surgical treatment options, techniques such as hook and plate, Bosworth screws, and single/double beam reconstruction have certain problems of over-concentration of short-term follow-up, small sample size, and incomplete reporting of complications. In the future, there is still a need for more multicenter, large-sample, long-term follow-up RCTs that incorporate patient-reported outcome metrics (PROMs) and complication rates. In the future, uniform quantitative criteria are developed to improve the consistency of staging and diagnostic decisions. Again, among the surgical treatment options, techniques such as hook and plate, Bosworth screws, and single/double beam reconstruction have certain problems of over-concentration of short-term follow-up, small sample size, and incomplete reporting of complications. In the future, there is still a need for more multicenter, large-sample, long-term follow-up RCTs that incorporate patient-reported outcome metrics (PROMs) and complication rates. Finally, in rehabilitation protocols, we point out that existing protocols are mostly based on expert consensus, lack of randomized controlled and comparative timing and intensity studies, and call for the design of controlled trials to assess the efficacy of different early activity and weight-bearing strategies. Based on these shortcomings, we conclude by summarizing the research gaps and suggesting future research directions that incorporate multimodal functional imaging, stratified population subgroups, and standardized endpoint design to enhance the comparability and clinical value of the studies. Furthermore, future research on surgical techniques should move beyond simple comparisons of “single-bundle versus double-bundle” and strive for stratified, patient-centered outcomes. As elucidated in this review, factors such as patient activity level, BMI, and the specific pattern of instability (vertical vs. horizontal) are critical determinants of success. Future randomized controlled trials (RCTs) must incorporate these variables into their design, comparing the efficacy of anatomically precise techniques (e.g., DCTa) against standard methods within specific patient subgroups. This will generate evidence that truly guides individualized surgical decision-making. A total of 22 clinical trials were searched on ClinicalTrials.gov using the keyword “acromioclavicular joint dislocation”. Based on the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 10 eligible studies were selected for analysis. These studies focused on the comparison of treatments for acute acromioclavicular joint dislocation, covered different surgical and non-surgical interventions, and reported relevant functional outcome measures. INCLUSION CRITERIA: Subjects: Adults (usually 18 to 65 years of age) with acute acromioclavicular joint dislocation, specifically types III to V of the Rockwood classification. Study design: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or prospective studies comparing the efficacy of different treatments (e.g., surgical vs. nonsurgical). STUDY STATUS: Study completed or currently recruiting with complete enrollment information on ClinicalTrials.gov. A total of 10 trials were included, of which the RCT with Hook plate fixation showed a mean improvement in Constant score of 7.8 points (95% CI 5.2–10.4, p = 0.03) at 6 months compared to conservative treatment, suggesting a short-term functional improvement advantage. Two double button versus Hook plate comparison trials did not show a significant difference (MD 1.2 points, 95% CI −2.3-4.7, p = 0.50), but double-bundle reconstruction performed more consistently in terms of CC gap maintenance. Three Bosworth screw studies reported screw fatigue fracture rates as high as 18% within 8–12 weeks postoperatively, suggesting questionable long-term reliability. Overall, these studies provide direct comparative data between different surgical and conservative strategies in terms of short-term function, stability and risk of complications, which can help to clinically individualize treatment plans for different Rockwood subtypes.” As one of the most common shoulder injuries, ACJ dislocation has a complex anatomy and slow functional recovery. It has always been a difficult problem for athletes and manual laborers. Currently, ACJ dislocations are categorized into six grades (from type I to type VI) according to the most commonly used Rockwood classification. Physical examination and imaging are essential to diagnose and classify ACJ dislocations, which are also classified according to disease severity as non-surgical (usually used for low-grade dislocations such as Types I and II) and surgical (for high-grade dislocations such as Types IV, V, and VI). The treatment of Type III dislocations is controversial and needs to be individualized according to the patient’s symptoms and clinical needs. In this review, we review in detail the anatomical basis of ACJ dislocations, possible pathogenesis, imaging evaluation, and treatment options. We also discussed in depth the possible complications of the treatment process and the subsequent rehabilitation process. The treatment and rehabilitation of ACJ subluxation need to be based on individualized evaluation and treatment protocols, as well as multidisciplinary collaboration. Future research should continue to explore new surgical techniques and rehabilitation methods to improve the efficacy of ACJ treatment, reduce the risk of complications, promote the recovery of shoulder function and ensure long-term patient satisfaction, thus maximizing the quality of life of patients. Methods: This manuscript is a narrative review aimed at summarizing and contextualizing current concepts in acromioclavicular joint (ACJ) dislocation, including anatomy, biomechanics, imaging, classification, treatment options, complications, and rehabilitation. The literature was identified through non-systematic, topic-driven searching of major databases and reference lists of relevant articles, with study selection guided by clinical relevance and recency rather than a pre-specified systematic-review protocol. To complement the narrative synthesis and provide an overview of ongoing and recently completed comparative research, we additionally performed a supplementary trial mapping using ClinicalTrials.gov. The registry was queried using the keyword “acromioclavicular joint dislocation” (search date: [insert date]). Trials were screened to identify studies most relevant to contemporary management of acute ACJ dislocation. Eligibility criteria were defined a priori for this registry mapping as follows: (1) adult participants with acute ACJ dislocation (typically Rockwood types III–V); (2) randomized controlled trials or prospective comparative studies evaluating. surgical versus nonoperative care or comparing surgical techniques; and (3) trials listed as completed or recruiting with adequate enrollment information and accessible outcome descriptions in the registry. This process identified 22 registered studies, of which 10 met the mapping criteria and were summarized descriptively. Because the objective of this component was descriptive characterization rather than quantitative synthesis, results were extracted and reported narratively, focusing on the type of intervention, comparator, follow-up, and reported functional or radiographic outcomes. No pooled meta-analysis was performed.
